words.shortDefinition: WebAssembly modules running on Kubernetes via containerd's runwasi shim; sub-millisecond cold starts, smaller attack surface than OCI containers.
words.simpleDefinition: WASM workloads on Kubernetes let you run tiny, sandboxed WebAssembly binaries alongside regular containers on the same cluster. SpinKube is the operator that manages Fermyon Spin WASM apps as a CRD, while the runwasi containerd shim handles execution. WASM modules start in under 1 ms, weigh 1-10 MB instead of 50-300 MB for container images, and enforce capability-based sandboxing without relying on Linux cgroups or seccomp.
words.longDefinition: WebAssembly (WASM) entered the Kubernetes world through two layers. At the bottom is runwasi — a CNCF sandbox containerd shim that routes OCI images annotated with `module.wasm.image/variant: compat` to a WASM runtime (Wasmtime or WASMedge) instead of runc. Kubernetes sees a normal pod; the runtime selects a different execution backend at the node level. SpinKube sits above this: it is a CNCF sandbox project providing a SpinApp CRD and operator for managing Fermyon Spin applications on Kubernetes, distributing WASM binaries as OCI artifacts and configuring the containerd-wasm-shim automatically. The core advantages of WASM over containers are cold-start latency (sub-1 ms versus 10-50 ms for a minimal container), image size (1-10 MB versus 50-300 MB), and the WASI capability sandbox — a WASM module without declared filesystem access cannot touch the filesystem regardless of kernel configuration. In 2026 WASM workloads on K8s are production-viable for stateless HTTP handlers and event processors written in Rust or Go. They are not suitable for workloads requiring POSIX threading, direct GPU access, or large language runtimes like Python or JVM.
words.connector: Think of WASM workloads like a vending machine dispenser next to a full restaurant kitchen — the vending machine (WASM) dispenses a snack in under a second from a sealed compartment; the kitchen (container) can cook anything but takes much longer to set up.
words.techContext: We switched our edge event processors from Alpine containers to SpinKube WASM modules and reduced cold-start latency from 40 ms to 0.8 ms while cutting image pull bandwidth by 95%.
words.exampleSentence: After deploying SpinKube, our WASM-based API handlers started in under a millisecond and the cluster scheduler treated them identically to regular OCI pods.

codeExample.code:
# SpinApp CRD (SpinKube)
apiVersion: core.spinoperator.dev/v1alpha1
kind: SpinApp
metadata:
  name: event-processor
spec:
  image: ghcr.io/myorg/event-processor:latest  # WASM OCI artifact
  replicas: 3
  executor: containerd-shim-spin  # runwasi shim
---
# RuntimeClass wiring
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: spin
handler: spin  # containerd shim handler

words.etymology: SpinKube: Spin is Fermyon's WASM framework; Kube is the standard abbreviation for Kubernetes. runwasi: run + WASI (WebAssembly System Interface), the system-call layer for WASM modules.

words.shortDefinition: Kernel-programmable networking and observability that replaces iptables/kube-proxy; XDP hooks give line-rate packet processing.
words.simpleDefinition: eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) lets you load small verified programs into the Linux kernel at specific hook points — packet ingress, socket syscalls, tracepoints — without writing a kernel module. In Kubernetes, Cilium uses eBPF to replace kube-proxy's iptables chains with O(1) hash-map lookups, enforce NetworkPolicy inside the kernel where containers cannot bypass it, and capture detailed L3/L4/L7 flow telemetry without sidecars.
words.longDefinition: The classical Kubernetes networking path sends every packet through iptables chains — a sequential linked list traversal. At 10,000 services and 50,000 pods a cluster can have hundreds of thousands of iptables rules; lookup time grows linearly with rule count. eBPF solves this at the kernel level: a restricted, safely-typed bytecode program is JIT-compiled and attached to kernel hook points (XDP for ingress before the network stack, TC for egress/ingress after, kprobes/tracepoints for observability). The kernel verifier guarantees the program terminates and cannot corrupt kernel memory. Cilium's eBPF-native implementation replaces kube-proxy with a BPF hash map for O(1) service IP lookup, compiles NetworkPolicy rules into BPF programs attached to each pod's veth interface (tamper-proof because enforcement is in the kernel), and captures L3/L4/L7 flow data via Hubble without any sidecar proxy. Cilium is the default CNI on GKE Dataplane V2 (since 2021), AWS EKS in eBPF mode (2023), and graduated from CNCF in 2023. It is the most significant low-level infrastructure shift in Linux networking since iptables replaced ipchains in 2001.
words.connector: Think of eBPF like a toll plaza that was replaced by an RFID lane: the old iptables model queued every car through a single booth and checked a paper list; eBPF runs a hash lookup that finds the exit in constant time, regardless of how many cars are on the road.
words.techContext: After replacing kube-proxy with Cilium's eBPF dataplane, our service-to-service latency at p99 dropped by 18% on a cluster with 8,000 services — the iptables chain traversal had been the hidden bottleneck.
words.exampleSentence: The eBPF dataplane let us enforce NetworkPolicy at the kernel level, making it impossible for a compromised container to manipulate iptables rules and bypass its own isolation.

codeExample.code:
# Install Cilium with kube-proxy replacement and Hubble
helm install cilium cilium/cilium \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --set kubeProxyReplacement=true \
  --set hubble.relay.enabled=true \
  --set hubble.ui.enabled=true \
  --set bpf.masquerade=true

# Verify kube-proxy replacement is active
cilium status --verbose | grep KubeProxyReplacement

words.etymology: eBPF: extended Berkeley Packet Filter. BPF originated as a packet-filtering language in 1992 (Steven McCanne and Van Jacobson). The 'extended' prefix was added in Linux 3.18 (2014) when Alexei Starovoitov dramatically widened the instruction set and added the in-kernel JIT compiler.

words.shortDefinition: eBPF-native service mesh that provides mTLS, L7 policy, and mutual authentication without sidecar proxies.
words.simpleDefinition: Cilium Service Mesh extends Cilium's eBPF dataplane to provide service mesh capabilities — mutual TLS between pods, L7 traffic policies, retries, and observability — without injecting an Envoy sidecar into every pod. Instead, a single per-node Envoy proxy handles L7 traffic for all pods on that node, and pure L3/L4 features are handled entirely in eBPF with no userspace proxy at all.
words.longDefinition: Traditional service meshes (Istio with per-pod Envoy sidecars) impose a measurable overhead: each sidecar container consumes 50-200 MB RAM and 0.5-2 vCPU per pod at scale. Cilium Service Mesh eliminates this by moving as much work as possible into eBPF kernel programs. For pure L3/L4 features (mTLS based on SPIFFE identities, connection-level policy), Cilium uses eBPF sockops programs that intercept socket calls directly — no userspace proxy in the datapath. For L7 features requiring HTTP/gRPC parsing, Cilium deploys one shared per-node Envoy proxy managed by Cilium itself, rather than one sidecar per pod; this reduces proxy instance count from O(pods) to O(nodes). Hubble provides full network flow visibility (DNS queries, HTTP method/status, gRPC service names) derived from eBPF hooks — the same observability signal that Istio's sidecar would provide, without the sidecar CPU/memory cost. Cilium Service Mesh targets teams that need mesh capabilities but cannot absorb the sidecar overhead, particularly at high pod densities or on memory-constrained edge nodes.
words.connector: Traditional service meshes work like giving every employee their own personal assistant (sidecar) who handles all their calls. Cilium Service Mesh instead puts one floor receptionist (per-node Envoy) and uses the building's intercom system (eBPF) for simple calls — dramatically reducing headcount while covering the same duties.
words.techContext: We moved from Istio sidecar injection to Cilium Service Mesh and reclaimed 40 GB of RAM across the cluster — the sidecar proxies had collectively consumed as much memory as our actual application containers.
words.exampleSentence: Cilium Service Mesh gave us mTLS between all services and per-request HTTP observability from Hubble without adding a single sidecar container to the cluster.

codeExample.code:
# Enable Cilium mutual authentication (mTLS via SPIFFE)
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-mtls
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: payments
  ingress:
    - fromEndpoints:
        - matchLabels:
            app: checkout
      authentication:
        mode: required  # enforce mTLS; deny unauthenticated

words.etymology: Cilium: named after the hair-like cellular structures (cilia) that move fluids — a metaphor for the network traffic the project manages. First open-sourced by Thomas Graf at Covalent (acquired by Isovalent, later acquired by Cisco) in 2016.

words.shortDefinition: Istio architecture (stable 2024) that removes per-pod Envoy sidecars, replacing them with node-level ztunnel proxies.
words.simpleDefinition: Ambient mesh is Istio's sidecar-free architecture. Instead of injecting an Envoy proxy into every pod, it deploys two components: a per-node ztunnel (zero-trust tunnel) that handles L4 mTLS and basic telemetry for all pods on the node, and an optional per-namespace waypoint proxy (also Envoy) for pods that need L7 features like HTTP routing and retries. Pods require no modification; ambient mesh is enabled at the namespace level.
words.longDefinition: Istio's classic sidecar model injects an Envoy proxy container into every pod. At scale this is expensive: hundreds of sidecar containers per cluster, each consuming CPU and RAM, all needing version-coordinated upgrades alongside the data plane. The operational pain — especially the requirement to restart every pod to upgrade a sidecar — drove the ambient mesh design, which reached stable status in Istio 1.22 (2024). Ambient mesh uses a two-tier architecture: the ztunnel DaemonSet (one pod per node, written in Rust) captures all pod traffic via eBPF socket redirection and provides L4 mutual TLS using SPIFFE/SPIRE identities and encrypted HBONE (HTTP-Based Overlay Network Encapsulation) tunnels between nodes — with no pod restart required when the ztunnel is upgraded. For services that need L7 capabilities (header-based routing, retries, JWT validation, gRPC load balancing), a waypoint proxy — a full Envoy instance — is deployed per namespace or per service account; only those services pay the L7 proxy cost. The result: zero per-pod overhead for most workloads, targeted L7 cost for workloads that need it, and decoupled upgrade cycles for infrastructure versus application pods.
words.connector: Think of ambient mesh like a city's bus system. Old Istio gave every commuter a personal driver (sidecar Envoy). Ambient mesh installs bus routes (ztunnel) that everyone shares for simple trips, and premium car service (waypoint proxy) for commuters who need door-to-door service — most people just use the bus.
words.techContext: Migrating to ambient mesh eliminated our most painful Kubernetes upgrade ceremony: rolling restarts across 400 Deployments to update sidecar proxy versions now happens as a single DaemonSet rollout.
words.exampleSentence: Ambient mesh let us enable mTLS across the entire cluster in minutes by labeling namespaces — no pod restarts, no sidecar injection, no per-pod resource overhead.

codeExample.code:
# Enable ambient mesh for a namespace (no pod restarts)
kubectl label namespace payments istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient

# Add a waypoint proxy for L7 features on the payments service account
istioctl waypoint apply --service-account payments-sa --namespace payments

# Verify ztunnel enrolled the pods
kubectl get pods -n payments -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.annotations}' \
  | grep -o 'ambient.istio.io/redirection: enabled'

words.etymology: Ambient: from Latin ambire, to go around — implying the mesh infrastructure surrounds workloads without being embedded in them. The architecture was announced by Istio maintainers (Google, Solo.io) at KubeCon NA 2022 and reached stable status in 2024.

words.shortDefinition: AWS open-source node provisioner that launches right-sized EC2 instances within seconds of scheduling demand, replacing Cluster Autoscaler.
words.simpleDefinition: Karpenter is a Kubernetes node provisioner (originally from AWS, now multi-cloud) that watches for unschedulable pods and launches the exact EC2 instance type that best fits them — within seconds, without pre-defined node groups. Unlike Cluster Autoscaler, Karpenter picks instance type and size at scheduling time, enabling spot-instance mixing, efficient bin-packing, and automatic consolidation of underutilised nodes.
words.longDefinition: Cluster Autoscaler scales pre-configured Auto Scaling Groups (ASGs) — you define the instance types up front and Cluster Autoscaler adjusts the count. This means you need separate ASGs for each instance type combination you might need, and scale-out involves launching a node from that group's fixed configuration. Karpenter discards the ASG model entirely. It registers as a Kubernetes controller, watches for pending pods whose resource requirements cannot fit existing nodes, computes the cheapest instance type across the full EC2 family (including spot) that satisfies the pod's requirements, and calls the EC2 CreateFleet API directly — a new node is registered and scheduling begins in under 60 seconds. Karpenter also runs a consolidation loop that detects underutilised nodes, cordons and drains them, and terminates the EC2 instance — reducing idle capacity without manual intervention. NodePool and NodeClass CRDs declare constraints (instance families, availability zones, AMI families, spot/on-demand preference); pods annotate themselves with requirements using standard `nodeAffinity` or Karpenter-specific labels. In 2026 Karpenter is the recommended autoscaler for new EKS deployments; providers for GKE and AKS are in active development.
words.connector: Cluster Autoscaler is like a restaurant that only has three fixed table sizes and calls the furniture store when every table of that size is full. Karpenter is like a restaurant that measures the arriving group and orders a custom table — no pre-set sizes, just the right fit.
words.techContext: After switching from Cluster Autoscaler to Karpenter, our average node utilisation rose from 52% to 78% because Karpenter bins-packs pods onto right-sized instances instead of launching the next node in a fixed ASG.
words.exampleSentence: Karpenter launched a c7g.4xlarge ARM spot instance within 45 seconds of a burst of unschedulable ML inference pods — three times faster than our old Cluster Autoscaler node group.

codeExample.code:
# Karpenter NodePool
apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1
kind: NodePool
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      requirements:
        - key: karpenter.sh/capacity-type
          operator: In
          values: [spot, on-demand]
        - key: kubernetes.io/arch
          operator: In
          values: [amd64, arm64]
      nodeClassRef:
        apiVersion: karpenter.k8s.aws/v1
        kind: EC2NodeClass
        name: default
  disruption:
    consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized
    consolidateAfter: 30s

words.etymology: Karpenter: portmanteau of Kubernetes and carpenter — the tool that builds and shapes the node fleet. Open-sourced by AWS at re:Invent 2021; donated to the CNCF as an Incubating project in 2024.

words.shortDefinition: Extends HPA to scale pods to zero based on external event sources (Kafka lag, SQS depth, Prometheus metrics).
words.simpleDefinition: KEDA is a CNCF-graduated Kubernetes controller that adds event-driven scaling to any Deployment, StatefulSet, or Job. Unlike the built-in HPA — which only understands CPU and memory — KEDA can scale workloads based on Kafka consumer lag, SQS queue depth, Redis list length, Prometheus query results, GitHub Actions queue size, and 60+ other sources. Critically, KEDA can scale all the way to zero replicas when the queue is empty, and back up when events arrive.
words.longDefinition: The standard Kubernetes HPA has a hard limitation: it can only scale on CPU utilization, memory, or custom metrics from the Metrics API. Event-driven workloads — Kafka consumers, SQS processors, webhook handlers — are not CPU-bound at idle; their correct replica count is proportional to the event backlog, not CPU usage. A Kafka consumer with an empty topic should run zero replicas; one with a million-message lag should run dozens. KEDA solves this by implementing two K8s objects: ScaledObject (for Deployments/StatefulSets) and ScaledJob (for batch Jobs-on-demand). A ScaledObject references one or more scalers — each scaler connects to an external system, reads a metric (e.g. Kafka consumer group lag for topic X), and returns a target replica count. KEDA then manages an HPA resource internally, keeping it in sync with the external metric. Scale-to-zero is KEDA's key innovation: when the external metric hits zero, KEDA bypasses the HPA minimum and deletes all replicas; on the next event, it starts pods and queues incoming messages. KEDA graduated from CNCF in 2023 and is the standard event-driven autoscaling solution for new Kubernetes deployments. It integrates natively with Azure, AWS, GCP, and every major message broker.
words.connector: KEDA is like a restaurant kitchen that reads the order queue — when there are 0 orders, all chefs go home; when 100 orders arrive, it calls in as many chefs as needed. The built-in HPA only knows how hot the stoves are, which is a poor proxy for how much cooking needs to be done.
words.techContext: KEDA eliminated our always-on Kafka consumer Deployments — at night the replica count drops to zero and we save 40% on our EKS compute bill, scaling back up within 30 seconds when morning batch events arrive.
words.exampleSentence: KEDA scaled our order processing Deployment from zero to twenty replicas within seconds of the first SQS message arriving, then back to zero once the queue drained.

codeExample.code:
# KEDA ScaledObject for a Kafka consumer
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata:
  name: order-processor
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    name: order-processor
  minReplicaCount: 0   # scale to zero
  maxReplicaCount: 30
  triggers:
    - type: kafka
      metadata:
        bootstrapServers: kafka:9092
        consumerGroup: order-processors
        topic: orders
        lagThreshold: '100'   # 1 replica per 100 messages of lag

words.etymology: KEDA: Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling. Created by Microsoft and Red Hat, first released in 2019, donated to CNCF as a Sandbox project in 2020, graduated in 2023.

words.shortDefinition: K8s 1.26+ API for structured GPU/accelerator requests and sharing, replacing opaque device plugin integer counts.
words.simpleDefinition: Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) is a Kubernetes API that lets workloads describe what they need from a hardware device — topology, capacity, sharing constraints — rather than just requesting an integer count. A ResourceClaim might ask for 'an NVIDIA GPU with at least 40 GB memory on the same PCIe fabric as the requested CPU socket.' The device driver's DRA plugin decides which specific device satisfies the claim, and multiple pods can share a device if the driver permits it.
words.longDefinition: The Kubernetes device plugin model (introduced in 1.8) exposed hardware resources as schedulable integers: `nvidia.com/gpu: 1` requests one GPU. This works for simple cases but breaks down for modern accelerator clusters where you need: two GPUs on the same NVLink fabric, a fractional GPU slice (MIG partition), or a network adapter on the same NUMA node as the CPU. The integer model cannot express any of these constraints. DRA (KEP-3063, Alpha in 1.26, Beta in 1.31, GA in 1.32) replaces device plugin integers with ResourceClaim objects. A ResourceClaim describes desired device properties using structured parameters. The device driver's DRA plugin maintains a DeviceClass and publishes ResourceSlice objects that describe available devices and their attributes. The scheduler matches claims to slices and binds the claim to a specific device before the pod is scheduled — ensuring placement respects hardware topology. In 1.32 the scheduler itself can evaluate structured parameters without requiring a driver webhook, improving scheduling throughput for large GPU clusters. DRA is the foundation for GPU time-slicing, MIG partition allocation, and multi-device job scheduling in the 2026 Kubernetes ecosystem.
words.connector: The old device plugin model is like a hotel that only tells you how many rooms are available. DRA is like a booking system that knows which rooms have a sea view, an interconnecting door, and are on the same floor — you describe what you need and the system finds the exact match.
words.techContext: After enabling DRA, our ML training jobs could request two GPUs on the same NVLink fabric in a single ResourceClaim — something we had been working around with custom node labeling and affinity rules for two years.
words.exampleSentence: DRA let our AI workload request a pair of NVLink-connected A100 slices in one ResourceClaim, and the scheduler bound it to the only node with that topology without any manual placement hints.

codeExample.code:
# DRA ResourceClaim for a GPU with topology constraint
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1alpha3
kind: ResourceClaim
metadata:
  name: training-gpu
spec:
  devices:
    requests:
      - name: gpu
        deviceClassName: nvidia.com/gpu
        selectors:
          - cel:
              expression: device.attributes['memory.gib'].isGreaterThan(quantity('40Gi'))
        count: 2
        allocationMode: ExactCount

words.etymology: Dynamic Resource Allocation: dynamic because the allocation decision happens at scheduling time based on live device inventory, not at cluster setup time. The KEP was authored by Patrick Ohly (Intel) and merged into K8s 1.26.

words.shortDefinition: Workloads running inside hardware-enforced TEEs (AMD SEV, Intel TDX) so even the host hypervisor cannot inspect memory.
words.simpleDefinition: Confidential containers run inside a hardware Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) — AMD SEV-SNP or Intel TDX — where the workload's memory is encrypted at the hardware level. Even the cloud provider, hypervisor, and cluster admin cannot read the container's in-use data. Remote attestation lets the tenant cryptographically verify that the workload is running on genuine TEE hardware before sending sensitive data to it.
words.longDefinition: Standard Kubernetes security protects data at rest (etcd encryption) and in transit (mTLS), but leaves data in use exposed: anyone with physical access to the host hardware — including the cloud provider — can read the RAM of any running VM or container. For regulated workloads handling healthcare records, financial data, or cryptographic key material, 'trust the cloud provider' is often an unacceptable compliance position. Confidential containers (a CNCF Sandbox project combining cloud-hypervisor, Kata Containers, and an attestation agent) address this by running each pod inside a hardware-encrypted VM. AMD SEV-SNP (available on AWS, Azure, GCP since 2022-2023) and Intel TDX (Sapphire Rapids, 2023+) encrypt the entire guest VM's memory with a key that never leaves the CPU package — the VMM sees only ciphertext. Remote attestation allows the workload to prove to an external party that it is running on genuine SEV/TDX hardware with an unmodified measurement, before secrets are provisioned into the TEE. In 2026 confidential containers add 5-15% performance overhead (memory encryption) and require attestation infrastructure (a key broker service). They are in production at regulated financial services and healthcare organizations on Azure DCasv5 and AWS instances with SEV. They do not protect against application vulnerabilities or malicious code inside the trust domain — they are one layer in a defense-in-depth model.
words.connector: Regular containers are like safety deposit boxes where the bank can read what is inside. Confidential containers are like a vault where the combination is inside your head — even the bank building's owner cannot access the contents, and you get a receipt proving the vault is genuine before you deposit anything.
words.techContext: We moved our HIPAA PHI processing workloads to confidential containers on Azure DCasv5 nodes — our compliance audit now has hardware attestation receipts proving the data was processed inside a TEE that our cloud provider cannot inspect.
words.exampleSentence: Confidential containers on AMD SEV-SNP nodes gave our fintech client the in-use encryption proof required by their financial regulator — something that neither RBAC nor encrypted etcd could provide.

codeExample.code:
# Pod using Kata Containers with confidential VM (TEE)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: confidential-processor
  annotations:
    io.containerd.cri.runtime-handler: kata-cc  # confidential containers handler
spec:
  runtimeClassName: kata-cc
  containers:
    - name: processor
      image: myorg/phi-processor:latest
      resources:
        limits:
          memory: 4Gi
          cpu: 2

words.etymology: Confidential computing: the term coined by the Confidential Computing Consortium (CCC, Linux Foundation, 2019) to describe hardware-enforced data-in-use protection. TEE (Trusted Execution Environment) predates this, appearing in ARM TrustZone documentation circa 2004.

words.shortDefinition: Lightweight virtual Kubernetes cluster running inside a namespace of a host cluster — soft multi-tenancy without node isolation.
words.simpleDefinition: vCluster creates a fully functional Kubernetes virtual cluster as a StatefulSet inside a host cluster namespace. Each virtual cluster runs its own API server (k3s or vanilla K8s), its own etcd, and its own controller manager — giving tenants a complete K8s API surface including CRDs, ClusterRoles, and admission webhooks. Workloads scheduled in the virtual cluster are synced down and actually run as pods on the host cluster's nodes.
words.longDefinition: Multi-tenancy on a shared Kubernetes cluster hits a ceiling when tenants need cluster-scoped resources: CRDs, ClusterRoles, MutatingWebhooks, or custom admission policies. Namespaces cannot scope these — a CRD is global, and a ValidatingWebhook affects the entire cluster. vCluster (Loft Labs) solves this by running a lightweight virtual control plane (k3s or full K8s) as a StatefulSet inside a host namespace. The virtual cluster has its own API server, scheduler, and etcd. When a tenant creates a Deployment in the virtual cluster, vCluster's syncer translates the resource and creates it in the host namespace under a prefixed name. From the tenant's perspective they have a full cluster; from the host's perspective they have a set of namespaced pods. This enables ephemeral per-PR clusters for CI, developer sandboxes with full cluster admin access, and SaaS products that need to ship 'managed Kubernetes' to customers. vCluster's security model is softer than separate clusters: the syncer bridges the virtual and host API surfaces, and a misconfigured sync rule can over-expose host resources. The default node/PV sync rules should be reviewed carefully for production multi-tenant deployments.
words.connector: vCluster is like a virtual machine running inside a VM: from inside the inner VM, you have the full OS experience; from outside, it is just a process. Virtual clusters give tenants the full Kubernetes API while remaining a workload from the host cluster's perspective.
words.techContext: Our CI system creates a fresh vCluster for each pull request, giving the test suite cluster-admin access to install CRDs and operators without polluting the shared staging cluster.
words.exampleSentence: The platform team provisioned vCluster instances for each product team — every team got cluster-admin access to install their own operators and CRDs without touching the shared host cluster.

codeExample.code:
# Create a virtual cluster in namespace 'team-payments'
vcluster create payments-dev \
  --namespace team-payments \
  --connect  # automatically kubeconfig to the virtual cluster

# From inside the virtual cluster: full API access
kubectl apply -f my-crd.yaml          # CRD scoped to virtual cluster
kubectl create clusterrolebinding ...  # ClusterRole inside virtual cluster

# Host cluster only sees synced pods in team-payments namespace
kubectl get pods -n team-payments --context host-cluster

words.etymology: vCluster: virtual cluster. Created by Loft Labs (now Loft) and open-sourced in 2021. The concept of virtual clusters was explored in Kubernetes SIG Multi-Tenancy from 2018 onward; vCluster was the first broadly adopted implementation.

words.shortDefinition: OCI-compatible registry mirror that turns cluster nodes into a P2P layer to eliminate pull bottlenecks during mass deploys.
words.simpleDefinition: Spegel is a peer-to-peer OCI registry mirror that runs as a DaemonSet. When a node needs to pull an image, Spegel checks whether any other node in the cluster already has the image layers, and serves them over a direct node-to-node connection instead of hitting the upstream registry. This eliminates the registry bandwidth bottleneck and rate limits during rolling deployments that restart hundreds of pods simultaneously.
words.longDefinition: Container registries become bottlenecks during mass deployments: a rolling update across 500 nodes that all pull a 200 MB image in parallel can saturate the registry's egress bandwidth or hit rate limits (DockerHub pulls, ECR throughput). Traditional registry mirrors (pull-through caches) centralise traffic to one mirror node, which itself becomes a single point of failure. Spegel (Swedish: mirror) takes a peer-to-peer approach. It runs as a DaemonSet and registers itself as a local containerd registry mirror on each node. When containerd needs an image layer, it first queries Spegel, which advertises available layers across all nodes using a distributed hash table. If any node already has the layer, it is served directly over an in-cluster HTTP connection. Spegel uses OCI Distribution Spec semantics — it is transparent to containerd and requires no changes to pod specs or image references. This makes it especially valuable for: node scale-out events (new nodes can pull from existing nodes), rolling deployments (later nodes pull from earlier nodes that already pulled), and DR scenarios where registry connectivity is degraded. Spegel was open-sourced by Philip Laine at XebiaLabs in 2023 and gained significant traction in 2024-2025 as a zero-config bandwidth optimisation.
words.connector: Spegel is like a neighbourhood WhatsApp group for software — instead of everyone ordering from the same pizza place at once and overwhelming it, you first check if a neighbour already has a pizza to share.
words.techContext: During a cluster-wide image rollout to 800 nodes, Spegel reduced our ECR egress bandwidth by 85% — nodes past the first dozen pulled layers peer-to-peer from nodes that had already completed the pull.
words.exampleSentence: Spegel's P2P distribution cut our rolling deployment time from 12 minutes to 3 minutes by letting later nodes in the rollout pull image layers directly from earlier nodes.

codeExample.code:
# Spegel DaemonSet install (helm)
helm install spegel oci://ghcr.io/spegel-org/helm-charts/spegel \
  --namespace spegel \
  --set spegel.registries[0]=https://ghcr.io \
  --set spegel.registries[1]=https://registry-1.docker.io \
  --set spegel.containerdRegistryConfigPath=/etc/containerd/certs.d

# Spegel automatically patches containerd mirror config on each node
# No changes to pod specs or image references required

words.etymology: Spegel: Swedish word for mirror — the project name reflects both the mirroring function and the Swedish origin of its creator, Philip Laine.

words.shortDefinition: ML-driven scheduler extensions that predict resource demand and pre-provision nodes before workload spikes arrive.
words.simpleDefinition: AI-augmented scheduling uses machine learning models to predict future resource demand and influence Kubernetes scheduling or node provisioning proactively — scaling nodes before pods become unschedulable, rather than reacting after. In 2026 this exists on a spectrum from proven (KEDA with time-series forecasting, VPA resource recommendations) to experimental (end-to-end ML schedulers that replace the kube-scheduler).
words.longDefinition: The default Kubernetes scheduler is deterministic and stateless: it evaluates one pod at a time against current node capacity without any model of historical demand or predicted future load. This means it cannot anticipate that a batch ML training job arrives every weekday at 2am and could have nodes pre-provisioned and warmed. AI-augmented scheduling addresses this gap across several maturity levels. At the proven tier: KEDA with time-series forecasting (e.g., a Prometheus query that predicts Kafka lag 5 minutes ahead) can trigger node provisioning before the first pod goes Pending; VPA's recommender uses historical usage data to set accurate CPU/memory requests — closing the under-request gap that causes pod OOM kills and the over-request gap that wastes cluster capacity; the Descheduler rebalances pods post-scheduling. At the experimental tier: Volcano (CNCF Incubating, used by ByteDance for ML training) adds gang scheduling and queue fairness for multi-pod jobs; academic work (DeepRM, Decima) trains reinforcement-learning schedulers. As of 2026, no open-source production-grade full-replacement ML scheduler exists. The operational risk of an unexplainable scheduling decision in a production cluster is a strong reason to keep the deterministic kube-scheduler and add ML at the capacity-planning and resource-recommendation layers only.
words.connector: The default scheduler is like a taxi dispatcher who only looks at which cars are currently available. AI-augmented scheduling is like a dispatcher who has studied three years of ride history and pre-positions cars in neighbourhoods where demand is about to spike — a few minutes ahead of the surge.
words.techContext: We used KEDA's predictive scaler with a Prometheus-based forecast query to pre-warm GPU nodes 10 minutes before our daily batch training job — eliminating the 8-minute cold-start wait that had been blocking our ML pipeline.
words.exampleSentence: AI-augmented scheduling in our cluster means node provisioning now starts ten minutes before our known traffic spike rather than three minutes after the first pod goes Pending.

# KEDA ScaledObject with Prometheus prediction query (AI-augmented)
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata:
  name: ml-training-prescaler
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    name: training-job-queue
  minReplicaCount: 0
  maxReplicaCount: 10
  triggers:
    - type: prometheus
      metadata:
        serverAddress: http://prometheus:9090
        # Forecast query: predict job_queue depth 10m ahead

words.etymology: AI-augmented scheduling: augment from Latin augere, to increase or enhance. The term distinguishes enhancement of the existing scheduler (adding ML signals) from replacement — a distinction that matters operationally in 2026.

words.shortDefinition: Serverless platform on Kubernetes that scales workloads to zero and back based on request traffic or event sources.
words.simpleDefinition: Knative is a CNCF Graduated project that adds serverless primitives to Kubernetes: scale-to-zero based on concurrent HTTP requests, revision-based traffic splitting for canary deployments, and an event routing system (Knative Eventing) for CloudEvents-based pub-sub. When zero requests are in flight the replica count drops to zero; the Knative activator buffers the next incoming request while a pod starts.
words.longDefinition: Knative consists of two largely independent components: Knative Serving and Knative Eventing. Knative Serving adds HTTP scale-to-zero to any container image. A Knative Service creates a Configuration (tracks desired state), a Route (traffic rules), and Revisions (immutable snapshots of the service configuration). Traffic is split across Revisions by percentage — the standard canary/A-B pattern without an Ingress controller plugin. Knative's autoscaler (KPA — Knative Pod Autoscaler) scales on concurrent requests per pod rather than CPU utilisation, which is a better signal for latency-sensitive HTTP handlers. The activator acts as a buffer: when all replicas are gone, it holds the next incoming connection while the first pod starts; once the pod is ready, the activator forwards the buffered request. Knative Eventing provides a CloudEvents broker-trigger model: producers emit events to a Broker; Triggers filter and route events to consumer services. This decouples producers from consumers via the CloudEvents standard, enabling event fan-out without tight coupling. The operational cost: Knative requires a networking layer (Istio, Kourier, or Contour) and adds 3-4 CRDs and controllers to the cluster. For teams that need HTTP traffic splitting and scale-to-zero, Knative is the mature answer; for teams that only need scale-to-zero from event queues, KEDA with the HTTP add-on is simpler.
words.connector: Knative is like a restaurant with staff who go home when there are no customers and are called in the moment a reservation arrives — the hostess (activator) greets the first guest and delays seating by two minutes while the chef (pod) rushes in.
words.techContext: Knative Serving let us ship ten low-traffic internal tools as scale-to-zero services — our idle compute bill for those tools dropped to near zero without changing a single line of application code.
words.exampleSentence: Knative's revision-based traffic splitting let us shift 5% of production traffic to the new checkout revision and monitor error rates before expanding to 100%, all declared in a single YAML update.

codeExample.code:
# Knative Service with traffic split across revisions
apiVersion: serving.knative.dev/v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: checkout
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      name: checkout-v2
    spec:
      containers:
        - image: myorg/checkout:v2
  traffic:
    - revisionName: checkout-v1
      percent: 95
    - revisionName: checkout-v2
      percent: 5

words.etymology: Knative: K (for Kubernetes) + native. Created by Google, IBM, Red Hat, and SAP; announced at Google Cloud Next 2018. The name emphasises that it is a native Kubernetes extension, not a separate platform.

words.shortDefinition: Service mesh that injects Envoy sidecars to provide mTLS, traffic management, retries, and distributed tracing cluster-wide.
words.simpleDefinition: Istio is a CNCF-graduated service mesh for Kubernetes that automatically injects an Envoy proxy sidecar into every pod in labeled namespaces. The sidecar intercepts all in/outbound traffic, enforcing mutual TLS (mTLS) between services, applying L7 traffic policies (retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, traffic splitting), and emitting Prometheus metrics and distributed traces — without application code changes.
words.longDefinition: Istio decomposes into a data plane (Envoy sidecars in each pod) and a control plane (istiod, a single binary combining Pilot for configuration, Citadel for certificate management, and Galley for config validation). istiod pushes xDS configuration to every Envoy proxy over gRPC, enabling cluster-wide changes — a new retry policy or a 10% canary weight shift — to propagate in seconds without pod restarts. Istio's key capabilities: automatic mTLS using SPIFFE X.509 certificates issued by istiod's built-in CA; VirtualService and DestinationRule CRDs that declare L7 routing rules (header matching, weight-based splitting, fault injection); AuthorizationPolicy CRDs for L4/L7 access control beyond Kubernetes NetworkPolicy; telemetry via Envoy access logs, Prometheus metrics, and W3C-standard distributed traces forwarded to Jaeger, Zipkin, or any OTLP backend. Istio graduated from CNCF in September 2022, affirming production readiness. Its primary operational challenge is the sidecar lifecycle: every Envoy version bump requires a rolling restart of all pods in the mesh. Ambient mesh (stable in 1.22) offers an escape from this constraint for teams running large pod fleets.
words.connector: Istio is like a building's communication and security infrastructure: every room automatically gets a standardised phone (Envoy sidecar) with built-in call logging, access control, and rerouting capability — no occupant has to wire their own system.
words.techContext: Istio's AuthorizationPolicy CRDs let us implement zero-trust networking in two days — we could enforce 'only the payments service may call the ledger service' without touching any application firewall rules or application code.
words.exampleSentence: Istio's VirtualService let us route 1% of production traffic to the new recommendation engine and measure its latency and error rate before promoting it to 100%.

# Istio canary traffic split
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: recommendations
spec:
  hosts:
    - recommendations
  http:
    - route:
        - destination:
            host: recommendations
            subset: stable
          weight: 99
        - destination:
            host: recommendations
            subset: canary
          weight: 1

words.etymology: Istio: from the Greek ιστίο (histio), meaning sail — evoking the steering and control of network traffic as a sail manages wind. Created by Google, IBM, and Lyft; open-sourced in 2017.

words.shortDefinition: GitOps continuous delivery tool that continuously syncs Kubernetes cluster state to manifests stored in a Git repository.
words.simpleDefinition: ArgoCD is a CNCF-graduated GitOps controller that watches Git repositories for Kubernetes manifests and continuously reconciles the live cluster to match. Any manual change to the cluster that diverges from Git is detected as drift. ArgoCD supports Helm, Kustomize, Jsonnet, and raw YAML, provides a rich web UI for deployment status, and supports multi-cluster sync from a single control plane.
words.longDefinition: ArgoCD implements the GitOps principle by running a reconciliation loop that periodically (or on webhook trigger) compares the desired state in a Git repo against the live state of a Kubernetes cluster. When they diverge, ArgoCD can auto-sync (apply the Git state) or alert for manual remediation. The central objects are Application (one Git path to one cluster namespace) and AppProject (access control and source/destination scoping). The App of Apps pattern uses one Application to manage a directory of child Application manifests — enabling a fleet of apps to be bootstrapped from a single Git commit. ArgoCD's multi-cluster mode runs a central ArgoCD instance that manages spoke clusters, each authenticated via a ServiceAccount token or OIDC; this is the standard fleet management pattern for large Kubernetes deployments. Health checks are first-class: ArgoCD evaluates resource health using built-in checks for Deployments, StatefulSets, Services, and custom Lua health scripts for CRDs. RBAC is built-in: roles map to ArgoCD projects, limiting which teams can sync to which clusters and namespaces. ArgoCD graduated from CNCF in December 2022 and is the most widely adopted GitOps tool in the K8s ecosystem as of 2026.
words.connector: ArgoCD is like a building manager who has a blueprint (Git) and walks the building every hour — if any room doesn't match the blueprint (someone moved a wall), the manager either calls maintenance to fix it or sends an alert.
words.techContext: ArgoCD's multi-cluster sync lets our platform team manage 40 production clusters from a single ArgoCD instance — every cluster's state is declared in Git and any manual kubectl change triggers a drift alert within 3 minutes.
words.exampleSentence: After a junior engineer accidentally deleted a CRD in production, ArgoCD detected the drift within two minutes and auto-synced it back from Git before any workloads were affected.

codeExample.code:
# ArgoCD Application syncing a Helm chart from Git
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/myorg/k8s-platform
    targetRevision: HEAD
    path: apps/payments-api
    helm:
      valueFiles:
        - values-production.yaml
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: payments
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true

words.etymology: ArgoCD: Argo is the mythological ship sailed by Jason and the Argonauts — evoking delivery through navigation. CD stands for Continuous Delivery. Created at Applatix (acquired by Intuit) in 2017; donated to CNCF in 2020.

words.shortDefinition: CNCF GitOps toolkit that reconciles Kubernetes clusters to manifests in Git, with support for Helm and Kustomize sources.
words.simpleDefinition: Flux is a CNCF-graduated GitOps toolkit composed of specialised controllers: the Source Controller watches Git repos, Helm repos, and OCI registries; the Kustomize Controller applies Kustomize overlays; the Helm Controller manages Helm releases; the Notification Controller triggers syncs from webhooks and sends alerts. Flux takes a composable toolkit approach rather than ArgoCD's monolithic application model.
words.longDefinition: Flux v2 (2021) was a ground-up rewrite of the original Flux (2016) using the GitOps Toolkit — a set of independent CNCF APIs and controllers that can be used together or separately. The four main controllers are: Source Controller (polls Git repositories, Helm chart repositories, OCI registries, and S3 buckets, producing Artifact objects); Kustomize Controller (applies Kustomizations — paths within a source — to clusters, with dependency ordering and health gating); Helm Controller (manages HelmRelease objects, delegating to Helm for chart rendering and release lifecycle); Notification Controller (handles inbound webhooks from GitHub/GitLab to trigger immediate reconciliation, and sends outbound alerts to Slack, PagerDuty, GitHub commit status). Flux's multi-tenancy model uses Kustomization dependencies and service accounts to isolate tenant reconciliation — each tenant's Kustomization runs as a dedicated service account with scoped RBAC. Flux graduated from CNCF in November 2022. Compared to ArgoCD, Flux has a stronger multi-tenancy story and tighter OCI artifact support; ArgoCD has a richer UI and more established multi-cluster fleet management. Many large organisations run both — ArgoCD for the platform team's cluster management, Flux for tenant application delivery.
words.connector: Flux is like a postal service with separate departments for each step — one team checks for new packages (Source Controller), one delivers Helm packages (Helm Controller), one assembles custom builds (Kustomize Controller), and one sends delivery notifications (Notification Controller).
words.techContext: We use Flux's OCI Source Controller to consume our Helm charts directly from our container registry as OCI artifacts, eliminating the separate Helm repository infrastructure we maintained.
words.exampleSentence: Flux's Kustomize Controller dependency ordering let us declare that the CRD Kustomization must reach Healthy status before any workload Kustomizations attempt to create CR instances.

kind: HelmRelease
metadata:

  namespace: cert-manager
spec:
  interval: 1h
  chart:
    spec:
      chart: cert-manager
      version: '>=1.14.0'
      sourceRef:
        kind: HelmRepository
        name: jetstack
  install:
    crds: CreateReplace
  upgrade:
    crds: CreateReplace

words.etymology: Flux: from Latin fluxus, meaning flow — the continuous flow of changes from Git to the cluster. Originally created by Weaveworks (2016); the v2 GitOps Toolkit was developed collaboratively with Microsoft and others; graduated from CNCF in 2022.

words.shortDefinition: eBPF-based Kubernetes security observability and enforcement runtime from the Cilium project that hooks into the Linux kernel to detect and block suspicious activity in real time.
words.simpleDefinition: Tetragon is a CNCF project (part of the Cilium ecosystem) that uses eBPF programs loaded into the Linux kernel to observe and optionally enforce security policies on Kubernetes workloads. Unlike audit-log-based tools that see events after the fact, Tetragon hooks at the kernel level: syscall entry/exit, network connections, file access. TracingPolicies define what to observe or block; events are exported as structured JSON or sent to an observability backend.
words.longDefinition: Tetragon runs as a DaemonSet on each node, loading eBPF programs via the kernel BPF subsystem at pod startup. Its architecture has two parts: sensors (eBPF programs hooking into kernel execution paths) and an in-kernel filtering and enforcement engine. Sensor hooks cover kprobes on Linux syscalls (open, connect, execve), LSM (Linux Security Module) hooks for enforcement, tracepoints on process lifecycle events (fork, exec, exit), and network socket hooks. Tetragon key capability is in-kernel enforcement: using eBPF LSM hooks, a TracingPolicy can terminate a process in-kernel before it completes a forbidden syscall, eliminating the time-of-check/time-of-use window that plagues userspace observe-and-kill approaches. TracingPolicies are Kubernetes CRDs. An example policy: deny any process in the production namespace from executing a shell. Events flow from the DaemonSet to an observability backend; Tetragon integrates with Hubble (Cilium observability layer), Elasticsearch, and any tool consuming JSON over gRPC or Unix socket. Each event carries Kubernetes context (pod name, namespace, labels, container ID) enriched at the kernel level, so every syscall event identifies exactly which pod triggered it. Tetragon was open-sourced by Isovalent in 2022 and became a CNCF Sandbox project.
words.connector: Think of Tetragon like a security system wired directly into every door lock in a building: it does not just record who enters, it can physically block a door from opening the moment a forbidden movement is detected, without routing through a management office that could be bypassed.
words.techContext: We deployed Tetragon with a TracingPolicy blocking shell execution in the production namespace. This stopped a compromised dependency from launching bash to exfiltrate credentials; the block happened in-kernel before the shell process could run.
words.exampleSentence: Tetragon in-kernel enforcement blocked a supply-chain attack that had bypassed our image scanner: the malicious library attempted to execve curl to exfiltrate a secret, and Tetragon killed the syscall before it completed.

codeExample.code:
# TracingPolicy: block shell execution in production namespace
apiVersion: cilium.io/v1alpha1
kind: TracingPolicy
metadata:
  name: block-shells-production
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      environment: production
  kprobes:
  - call: "sys_execve"
    syscall: true
    args:
    - index: 0
      type: "string"
    selectors:
    - matchArgs:
      - index: 0
        operator: "Prefix"
        values:
        - "/bin/sh"
        - "/bin/bash"
        - "/usr/bin/sh"
      matchActions:
      - action: Sigkill

words.etymology: Tetragon from Greek tetragonon ('four-cornered, square'). The Cilium team at Isovalent continues a tradition of Greek geometric names (Cilium, Hubble). Released as open source in 2022.

words.shortDefinition: Kubernetes extension that runs and manages virtual machines alongside containers in the same cluster, using KVM and the standard Kubernetes API.
words.simpleDefinition: KubeVirt adds VM support to Kubernetes without replacing the container model. You define a VirtualMachine or VirtualMachineInstance as a Kubernetes CRD, and KubeVirt runs it as a pod containing a KVM hypervisor process (libvirt/QEMU). VMs share Kubernetes storage (PVCs), networking (CNI), and scheduling (node affinity, resource requests). This lets teams managing legacy workloads, Windows applications, or security-isolated environments handle VMs with the same kubectl and GitOps workflows as containers.
words.longDefinition: KubeVirt was started by Red Hat in 2016 and is a CNCF Incubating project. It runs as a Kubernetes operator: a DaemonSet installs the virt-handler agent on each node, a Deployment runs the virt-controller, and a virt-api webhook validates VM manifests. When you create a VirtualMachine resource, the controller creates a corresponding VirtualMachineInstance; the virt-handler on the selected node sets up the QEMU/KVM process inside a pod (the virt-launcher pod), which shares the pod network namespace with the VM. The virtual NIC connects to the same CNI network as other pods so the VM can reach services using standard Kubernetes DNS. Storage is presented via PVCs and DataVolumes, a KubeVirt CRD that handles downloading and importing disk images into PVCs. Live migration between nodes is supported via a dedicated migration network. VM lifecycle operations: start, stop, pause, restart, live-migrate are all expressed as patches to the VirtualMachine CRD or via the virtctl CLI. VirtualMachineInstanceReplicaSet scales identically configured VMIs like a ReplicaSet scales pods. KubeVirt is the foundation of OpenShift Virtualization and is used in bare-metal Kubernetes environments where replacing all VMs with containers immediately is impractical.
words.connector: Think of KubeVirt like adding a VM track to a container train station: the scheduler treats VMs and containers as different carriage types but routes them on the same tracks, using the same ticketing system (kubectl), storage bays (PVCs), and departure board (the API server).
words.techContext: We run legacy Windows license-server VMs in KubeVirt alongside Linux microservices on the same cluster, sharing the same Cilium CNI network and scheduled by the same admission webhooks, eliminating the separate VMware estate and its associated operational overhead.
words.exampleSentence: KubeVirt live migration moved our database VM off a failing node during a hardware repair window with zero downtime, the same capability that previously required vMotion licenses and a dedicated VMware cluster.
