apiVersion: kubevirt.io/v1
kind: VirtualMachine
metadata:
  name: legacy-windows-server
  namespace: platform
spec:
  running: true
  template:
    spec:
      domain:
        cpu:
          cores: 4
        memory:
          guest: 8Gi
        devices:
          disks:
          - name: system-disk
            disk:
              bus: virtio
      volumes:
      - name: system-disk
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: windows-server-pvc
---
# Live-migrate a running VM to another node
# virtctl migrate legacy-windows-server

words.etymology: Kube from Kubernetes (Greek kubernetes, 'helmsman, governor'); Virt from Virtualization (Latin virtualis, 'potential'). KubeVirt directly names its function: virtualization for Kubernetes.

words.shortDefinition: Runtime security tool using eBPF/kernel module to detect anomalous syscall behaviour inside running containers.
words.simpleDefinition: Falco is a CNCF-graduated runtime security tool that monitors Linux system calls made by every container on a node. Using eBPF probes or a kernel module, it intercepts syscalls in real-time and evaluates them against a rule set. When a container does something unexpected — spawns a shell, reads /etc/shadow, opens a network socket from a binary that should not network — Falco emits an alert to Slack, PagerDuty, a SIEM, or any webhook.
words.longDefinition: Static security scanning (image scanning, admission webhooks) catches known bad patterns at deploy time. Falco addresses what happens after deployment: detecting anomalous behaviour in running containers in real time. It instruments the kernel's system call interface using either a loadable kernel module or an eBPF probe (preferred since Falco 0.28, as eBPF probes are safer than kernel modules in production). Every container syscall — open(), execve(), connect(), read() — passes through Falco's probe, which applies a rules engine. Default rules detect: spawning a shell inside a container (`execve` to bash/sh), privilege escalation (`setuid` syscall), reading sensitive files (/etc/shadow, /etc/kubernetes/pki/), network connections from unexpected binaries, and writing to `/etc` or kernel directories. Custom rules can be written in YAML using a macro/list/rule syntax. Falco outputs alerts as JSON events with full context (container id, pod name, namespace, process lineage, syscall arguments). FalcoSidekick is the companion tool that routes these events to 50+ destinations. Falco graduated from CNCF in January 2024. It is the most widely adopted runtime security tool in the Kubernetes ecosystem and is commonly deployed as a DaemonSet.
words.connector: Falco is like a building security guard who watches the cameras 24/7, not just at the entrance. Static security tools check ID at the door; Falco watches what everyone does once they are inside the building and raises an alarm if someone opens a server room they have no business in.
words.techContext: Falco's eBPF probe caught a compromised container trying to read /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.key within 200 milliseconds — the alert fired in Slack before the attacker could exfiltrate the credential.
words.exampleSentence: After deploying Falco, we detected three containers spawning shells inside production within the first week — all turned out to be developer debug sessions via kubectl exec that should not have been happening in prod.

codeExample.code:
# Falco custom rule: detect kubectl exec into production pod
- rule: Shell spawned in production container
  desc: A shell was spawned inside a container in the production namespace
  condition: >
    spawned_process and
    container.namespace = "production" and
    proc.name in (shell_binaries)
  output: >
    Shell spawned in production container
    (user=%user.name container=%container.name
     pod=%k8s.pod.name ns=%k8s.ns.name
     parent=%proc.pname cmd=%proc.cmdline)
  priority: WARNING
  tags: [container, shell, security]

words.etymology: Falco: named after the falcon — a fast, sharp-eyed predator used historically for hunting. Sysdig (the creator) chose the name to evoke rapid detection and precise targeting of threats. Open-sourced in 2016; CNCF Sandbox in 2018; graduated in 2024.

words.shortDefinition: Kubernetes operator that automates TLS certificate issuance and renewal from Let's Encrypt and other ACME CAs.
words.simpleDefinition: cert-manager is a Kubernetes operator that manages the full lifecycle of TLS certificates. It watches Certificate CRD objects, requests certificates from configured Issuers (Let's Encrypt, HashiCorp Vault, Venafi, self-signed), stores them as Kubernetes Secrets, and automatically renews them before expiry. It integrates with Ingress and Gateway API resources to provision TLS certificates based on hostname annotations.
words.longDefinition: Manual TLS certificate management in Kubernetes is error-prone at scale: certificates expire silently, private keys are stored inconsistently, and rotation requires coordinated changes across services. cert-manager solves this by treating certificates as Kubernetes-native objects. An Issuer (namespace-scoped) or ClusterIssuer (cluster-scoped) defines a certificate authority and challenge mechanism — ACME DNS-01 or HTTP-01 for Let's Encrypt, CSR-based for internal CAs, or a Vault PKI secrets engine. A Certificate object declares the desired certificate: common name, SANs, duration, renewal threshold. cert-manager's controller watches for expiring certificates (default: renew at 2/3 of lifetime), sends a CertificateRequest to the Issuer, completes the ACME challenge (modifying a DNS TXT record or creating an HTTP challenge pod), and stores the resulting cert and key in a Kubernetes Secret. The annotationated Ingress controller integration means adding `cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod` to an Ingress triggers automatic certificate provisioning for all hostnames in that Ingress. cert-manager is deployed in the majority of production Kubernetes clusters that serve HTTPS traffic, and is the reference implementation for Kubernetes Certificate API (certificates.k8s.io). It reached v1.0 in October 2020 and is now a CNCF Incubating project.
words.connector: cert-manager is like a passport renewal service that knows when your passport is about to expire, automatically submits the renewal application to the government, and places the new passport in your desk drawer before the old one runs out — you only had to file for the service once.
words.techContext: cert-manager eliminated our quarterly certificate rotation fire drill — 200 service certificates across our clusters now renew automatically, and we get a Slack alert only if a renewal fails.
words.exampleSentence: cert-manager's ClusterIssuer provisioned valid Let's Encrypt certificates for 45 Ingress hostnames automatically; our platform team went from spending 4 hours per quarter on cert rotation to zero.

codeExample.code:
# ClusterIssuer: Let's Encrypt production
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: platform@myorg.com
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-prod-account-key
    solvers:
      - http01:
          ingress:
            ingressClassName: nginx
---
# Ingress with automatic cert provisioning
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: api-gateway
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  tls:
    - hosts: [api.myorg.com]
      secretName: api-tls

words.etymology: cert-manager: certificate manager. Created by Jetstack (acquired by Venafi in 2022) in 2017; CNCF Incubating project since 2022. The lowercase naming follows Kubernetes ecosystem conventions (kubectl, helm, etc.).

words.shortDefinition: Cilium's eBPF-powered network observability layer providing packet-level flow telemetry and service dependency maps.
words.simpleDefinition: Hubble is Cilium's built-in network observability component. It uses eBPF hooks to capture L3/L4/L7 flow data — TCP connections, HTTP requests, DNS queries, gRPC calls — from every pod on every node, without injecting any sidecar proxy. A central Hubble Relay aggregates flows from all nodes; the Hubble UI renders live service maps showing which services talk to which, with flow counts, error rates, and latency.
words.longDefinition: Traditional Kubernetes network observability requires either sidecar proxies (Istio/Envoy collecting access logs) or packet capture (tcpdump, requiring privileged containers). Hubble provides the same depth of visibility using eBPF kernel hooks — at the kernel socket and network interface level, before packets reach userspace. The Hubble Observer runs as part of each Cilium agent DaemonSet pod; it taps into the same BPF maps that Cilium uses for policy enforcement, reading flow metadata (source/dest IP, port, HTTP method, gRPC service, DNS name, response code, latency). This data is aggregated by Hubble Relay into a cluster-wide gRPC API. Hubble CLI (`hubble observe`) provides tcpdump-style flow inspection filtered by namespace, pod, label, or protocol. Hubble UI auto-generates a service dependency map from observed flows — showing in real time which services communicate, with drop rates and error percentages on each edge. Critically, Hubble does not require application instrumentation: flows are captured at the network layer regardless of whether the application uses OTel, Envoy, or has any observability code at all. This makes it invaluable for auditing unknown traffic patterns, debugging intermittent connection drops, and generating service topology maps for legacy applications that were not designed with observability in mind.
words.connector: Hubble is like a wiretap built into the building's telephone exchange — rather than asking each room to keep its own call log (sidecar), the exchange records all call metadata for every room automatically, at the infrastructure level.
words.techContext: Hubble's service map revealed that a legacy batch job was making 50,000 direct database connections per minute — a pattern no one knew about, invisible to our application metrics, that was starving the database connection pool.
words.exampleSentence: Hubble's flow observability showed us the exact TCP error code and latency spike between the payment service and the ledger API, without any application log changes — we diagnosed a network policy misconfiguration in 10 minutes.

codeExample.code:
# Observe HTTP flows between namespaces in real time
hubble observe \
  --namespace payments \
  --protocol http \
  --verdict DROPPED \
  --output json | jq '{src:.source.namespace, dst:.destination.namespace, url:.l7.http.url, status:.l7.http.code}'

# Generate service dependency map for the payments namespace
hubble observe --namespace payments --last 1000 \
  | jq -r '[.source.labels["k8s:app"], .destination.labels["k8s:app"]] | @csv' \
  | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20

words.etymology: Hubble: named after astronomer Edwin Hubble, who mapped distant galaxies — Cilium's Hubble maps distant service-to-service connections across the cluster. The naming follows the Cilium team's space theme (Cilium itself refers to microscopic cilia; Hubble to cosmic observation).

words.shortDefinition: Kubernetes-native control plane that provisions and manages cloud infrastructure through CRDs and reconciliation loops, treating external cloud resources as Kubernetes objects.
words.simpleDefinition: Crossplane is a CNCF project that extends Kubernetes into a universal control plane for cloud infrastructure. You install Crossplane, add a provider (AWS, GCP, Azure, Terraform), then create cloud resources such as RDS databases, S3 buckets, or VPCs by applying YAML manifests. Crossplane reconciliation continuously ensures real-world infrastructure matches declared state. Composite Resources let platform teams define opinionated abstractions that application teams consume without knowing the underlying cloud details.
words.longDefinition: Crossplane was created by Upbound (open-sourced 2018, CNCF Incubation 2020, CNCF Graduation 2024) to bring the Kubernetes reconciler pattern to infrastructure provisioning. The architecture has three layers. Providers are Crossplane packages (OCI images) containing CRD definitions and controllers for a cloud platform: the AWS provider defines hundreds of CRDs such as RDSInstance, S3Bucket, VPC; the Terraform provider wraps any Terraform module. Managed Resources (MRs) are low-level CRDs mapping one-to-one to cloud API resources. Composite Resources (XRs) and Composite Resource Definitions (XRDs) let platform teams define higher-level abstractions that compose multiple MRs: a PostgreSQLInstance XR might provision an RDS instance, a parameter group, a security group, and a Secrets Manager secret as a single unit. Compositions are the templates that map XR fields to underlying MR fields, with patches and transforms for value mapping. Application teams create Claims (namespace-scoped) that bind to XRs (cluster-scoped), getting infrastructure without needing cloud API credentials or knowledge of the underlying composition. The reconciler continuously watches for drift between the Kubernetes spec and actual cloud resource state and corrects it, similar to how a Deployment controller ensures the right number of pods are running.
words.connector: Think of Crossplane like adding a universal remote control to your Kubernetes cluster: instead of reaching for separate cloud consoles or Terraform CLIs, you describe what you want in YAML and the same kubectl you already use provisions the database, bucket, and network, keeping them in sync with the spec indefinitely.
words.techContext: Our platform team publishes a PostgreSQLInstance Composite Resource that provisions an RDS instance with encryption, automated backups, and a randomly generated password Secret injected into the namespace. Application teams apply a 10-line YAML Claim and get a production-ready database without touching the AWS console.
words.exampleSentence: A Crossplane composition made it impossible for application teams to accidentally create an unencrypted S3 bucket: the XR template hardcodes encryption settings, so the only path to creating a bucket enforces the policy automatically.

codeExample.code:
# Crossplane Claim: request a managed PostgreSQL database
apiVersion: platform.example.com/v1alpha1
kind: PostgreSQLInstance
metadata:
  name: orders-db
  namespace: production
spec:
  parameters:
    storageGB: 20
    version: "14"
    region: us-east-1
  compositionSelector:
    matchLabels:
      provider: aws
      env: production
  writeConnectionSecretToRef:
    name: orders-db-conn   # Crossplane writes host/user/pass here

words.etymology: Cross from Old English cros ('a crossing, intersection') suggesting a surface spanning multiple planes; Plane from the idea of a control plane. Upbound chose the name to evoke a single control surface crossing multiple cloud providers.

words.shortDefinition: Kernel primitives (pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user) that give each container an isolated view of processes, network, and filesystem.
words.simpleDefinition: Linux namespaces are kernel features that partition global system resources so each process group sees its own isolated version. A container uses a set of namespaces to believe it is alone on the machine: its own process tree (pid namespace), its own network stack (net namespace), its own filesystem mounts (mnt namespace), its own hostname (uts namespace), its own IPC primitives (ipc namespace), and optionally its own user ID mapping (user namespace). All containers on a host share the same kernel — namespaces are the isolation layer, not virtualisation.
words.longDefinition: Linux namespaces were introduced incrementally: mount namespaces in Linux 2.4.19 (2002), UTS and IPC in 2.6.19 (2006), PID and network in 2.6.24 (2008), user namespaces in 3.8 (2013), cgroup namespaces in 4.6 (2016), and time namespaces in 5.6 (2020). Each namespace type wraps a different class of kernel resource. The six types relevant to containers: PID namespace — process IDs start at 1 inside the container; processes outside cannot be seen or killed; NET namespace — the container has its own network interfaces, routing tables, and iptables rules; the veth pair bridges it to the host; MNT namespace — the container has its own mount table; the container image's overlay filesystem is mounted here; UTS namespace — hostname and domain name are isolated; each container can have a distinct hostname; IPC namespace — System V IPC primitives (semaphores, message queues, shared memory) are isolated; USER namespace — UIDs/GIDs inside the container map to different UIDs/GIDs on the host, enabling a rootless container where UID 0 inside maps to an unprivileged UID outside. Container runtimes (runc, containerd) call `clone(2)` with the appropriate `CLONE_NEW*` flags to create these namespaces before exec-ing the container process. Understanding namespaces is required to reason about container escape vulnerabilities — every container escape exploits a namespace isolation failure, typically in the kernel itself or in a misconfigured user namespace.
words.connector: Linux namespaces are like the privacy screens in an open-plan office — each booth (container) has its own phone, its own desk layout, its own nameplate, and cannot see what the neighbouring booths are doing. All booths still share the same building structure (kernel).
words.techContext: During a security audit we discovered a pod running with hostPID: true — it could see all processes on the node because it was in the host PID namespace rather than its own, a namespace isolation misconfiguration that bypassed our network policies entirely.
words.exampleSentence: Understanding Linux namespaces explained why a container escape in our cluster reached the host — the runtime had been configured with shareProcessNamespace: true, placing two containers in the same PID namespace.

codeExample.code:
# Demonstrate namespace isolation with unshare(1)
# New PID + mount namespace: process tree starts at PID 1
sudo unshare --pid --mount --fork --mount-proc /bin/bash
ps aux  # shows only this bash and ps — isolated PID namespace

# Inspect namespaces of a running container
pid=$(docker inspect --format '{{.State.Pid}}' my-container)
ls -la /proc/$pid/ns/
# lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root pid:[4026532199]
# lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root net:[4026532201]
# lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root mnt:[4026532197]

words.etymology: Namespace: from the programming concept of a named scope for identifiers. Linux namespaces extend this to kernel resources. The term and initial implementation came from Eric Biederman's work on Linux VServers in the early 2000s.

words.shortDefinition: Linux kernel resource accounting hierarchy; enforces CPU, memory, and I/O limits for container processes.
words.simpleDefinition: Control Groups (cgroups) are a Linux kernel mechanism for organising processes into hierarchical groups and enforcing resource limits on each group. Every container runs in its own cgroup subtree. The kernel tracks CPU time, memory usage, and block I/O for each cgroup and enforces the limits declared in the container spec — a container that exceeds its memory limit is OOM-killed; a container that exceeds its CPU limit is throttled.
words.longDefinition: cgroups were merged into Linux 2.6.24 (2008) by Paul Menage and Rohit Seth from Google, who needed a way to enforce resource isolation for Google's internal container workloads. cgroups v1 organised resources by controller (cpu, memory, blkio, cpuset, devices, pids) with independent hierarchies per controller. cgroups v2 (merged in Linux 4.5, 2016; the default on modern distributions since ~2021) unifies all controllers into a single hierarchy with cleaner delegation semantics and improved memory accounting. In Kubernetes: the kubelet translates a pod's `resources.limits` into cgroup settings. A container with `memory: 512Mi` limit gets a `memory.max = 536870912` in its cgroup; when it exceeds this, the kernel's OOM killer terminates a process in the cgroup and Kubernetes logs an OOMKilled event. CPU limits are enforced via the CFS scheduler's `cpu.max` (v2) — a container limited to 0.5 CPU gets 50% of a core's time quota per scheduling period. CPU requests (not limits) set `cpu.shares` (v1) / `cpu.weight` (v2), which influence scheduling priority when the node is CPU-contended. cgroup namespaces (a separate kernel feature) give containers an isolated view of the cgroup hierarchy — a container cannot see that it is inside a parent cgroup. Understanding cgroups is essential for reasoning about QoS classes, OOM events, and CPU throttling — the three most common performance failure modes in Kubernetes workloads.
words.connector: cgroups are like the utility meters in a block of apartments — each apartment (container) has its own electricity and water meter, and a circuit breaker (memory limit) that trips if the tenant exceeds their allowed draw, preventing one apartment from starving the whole building.
words.techContext: After enabling cgroup v2 on our EKS nodes, our memory accounting became much more accurate — cgroup v2's unified memory accounting catches page cache attribution that v1's per-controller model missed, reducing spurious OOMKilled events by 40%.
words.exampleSentence: The container was OOMKilled because its cgroup memory limit was set to 256 Mi but the JVM heap alone needed 400 Mi — a cgroup enforcement that appeared as an application crash rather than an out-of-memory error in the app logs.

codeExample.code:
# Inspect cgroup v2 limits for a running container
pid=$(docker inspect --format '{{.State.Pid}}' my-java-app)
cgroup_path=$(cat /proc/$pid/cgroup | awk -F: '{print $3}')

# Memory limit enforced by kernel
cat /sys/fs/cgroup${cgroup_path}/memory.max
# 268435456  (256 MiB)

# CPU quota: container gets 50% of one core per 100ms period
cat /sys/fs/cgroup${cgroup_path}/cpu.max
# 50000 100000  (50ms out of every 100ms)

words.etymology: Control Groups: descriptive name for the resource grouping and control functionality. Originally called 'process containers' by Paul Menage in 2006; renamed to cgroups to avoid confusion with Linux Containers (LXC). cgroups v2 was designed by Tejun Heo and merged in 2016.

words.shortDefinition: Spectrum of K8s isolation strategies: shared namespace (soft), vCluster (virtual), separate cluster (hard).
words.simpleDefinition: Kubernetes multi-tenancy exists on a spectrum of isolation strength. Namespace-level tenancy (soft) uses RBAC and ResourceQuota to scope teams on a shared cluster but offers no kernel isolation. vCluster (virtual) gives each tenant a full Kubernetes API surface including CRDs, running as a workload inside the host cluster. Separate clusters (hard) provide complete control-plane and node isolation at the cost of per-cluster operational overhead.
words.longDefinition: Kubernetes was not designed for multi-tenancy — a namespace provides resource naming isolation but shares the control plane, API server, etcd, and underlying nodes. Choosing the right isolation tier requires matching the threat model and operational budget: Soft multi-tenancy (namespace per team) is appropriate for mutually trusting internal teams. RBAC restricts API access; ResourceQuota caps consumption; NetworkPolicy limits lateral movement; LimitRange enforces defaults. Does not prevent container escapes (a kernel exploit on one tenant's pod can affect all pods on the node) and does not prevent a privileged tenant from affecting cluster-level resources. Capsule (CNCF Sandbox, Clastix) groups namespaces into Tenant objects, allowing self-service namespace creation within tenant boundaries — a practical enhancement for large-enterprise soft tenancy. vCluster tenancy gives each tenant a full virtual Kubernetes cluster running as a StatefulSet in the host namespace. Tenants get their own API server, their own CRDs, their own ClusterRoles, their own admission webhooks — the full cluster API surface. Appropriate when tenants need cluster-scoped resources or full admin access without affecting other tenants. Still shares host nodes — a node-level exploit escapes the vCluster. Separate cluster tenancy provides the only true hard isolation: independent control planes, independent nodes, no shared fate. Managed by fleet tools (ArgoCD multi-cluster, Cluster API). The cost: each cluster requires its own upgrade, certificate management, and monitoring. The correct choice is the minimum isolation tier that satisfies the threat model, compliance requirements, and operational capacity — defaulting to separate clusters for all teams is often infeasible.
words.connector: Multi-tenancy tiers are like housing arrangements: namespace tenancy is a shared house (same kitchen, separate bedrooms); vCluster is a studio apartment in a converted warehouse (your own front door but shared building); separate clusters are detached houses (complete independence, separate utility bills).
words.techContext: Our internal platform uses namespace tenancy for product teams (trusted) and vCluster for external partners who need to install their own CRDs — we reserve separate clusters only for our regulated healthcare clients who require hard compliance boundaries.
words.exampleSentence: When a product team needed to install a custom CRD without waiting for platform team review, we provisioned them a vCluster in under two minutes — giving full cluster-admin in their virtual environment without touching the shared cluster.

codeExample.code:
# Soft tenancy: Capsule Tenant with self-service namespace creation
apiVersion: capsule.clastix.io/v1beta2
kind: Tenant
metadata:
  name: team-payments
spec:
  owners:
    - name: payments-team-admin
      kind: User
  namespaceOptions:
    quota: 5           # max 5 namespaces for this tenant
  resourceQuotas:
    scope: Tenant
    items:
      - hard:
          requests.cpu: '20'
          requests.memory: 40Gi
  networkPolicies:
    items:
      - podSelector: {}
        policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
        egress:
          - to: [{namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {capsule.clastix.io/tenant: team-payments}}}]

words.etymology: Multi-tenancy: multi (many) + tenant (from Old French tenant, holder/occupant). The concept migrated from SaaS product design into Kubernetes platform engineering as clusters became shared infrastructure for multiple teams.

words.shortDefinition: Lightweight CNCF service mesh using Rust-based micro-proxies; lower overhead than Envoy-based meshes, simpler ops model.
words.simpleDefinition: Linkerd is a CNCF-graduated service mesh that injects a tiny Rust-based proxy (linkerd-proxy, ~10 MB, ~5 ms P99 latency overhead) as a sidecar into every pod. It provides automatic mTLS between all meshed services, per-route golden-signal metrics, retries, timeouts, and traffic splitting — without requiring Envoy, Lua, or complex CRDs. Its operational simplicity is its primary differentiator versus Istio.
words.longDefinition: Linkerd 1.0 (2016, Scala/JVM) was the first service mesh for Kubernetes. Linkerd 2.0 (2018, Rust) was a complete rewrite targeting low overhead and operational simplicity. The proxy — linkerd-proxy — is a 10 MB Rust binary with a ~3-5 ms P99 latency addition (versus 10-30 ms for Envoy under load) and ~10 MB RAM per proxy versus 50-100 MB for Envoy. This makes Linkerd significantly cheaper at high pod densities. Feature set: automatic mTLS between all meshed pods using SPIFFE certificates issued by the Linkerd control plane's built-in CA; per-route HTTP/gRPC metrics (success rate, RPS, P99 latency) exposed as Prometheus metrics; configurable retries and timeouts on HTTPRoute objects; traffic splitting for canary deployments; multi-cluster support via the Linkerd multicluster extension. Linkerd deliberately excludes some Istio features: no Lua scripting, no ext_authz integration, no WebAssembly plugin filters, no complex VirtualService routing DSL. This is a feature for teams who find Istio's configurability to be operational complexity. The Linkerd control plane (destination, identity, proxy-injector) runs as a small Deployment set and has no external dependencies. Linkerd 2.12+ supports the Kubernetes Gateway API for HTTPRoute configuration. Graduated from CNCF in July 2021, Linkerd is the second most deployed service mesh after Istio, and is particularly popular in financial services and healthcare where the low-overhead proxy is a compliance-friendly choice.
words.connector: Linkerd versus Istio is like choosing between a specialist scalpel (Linkerd — precise, lightweight, limited range) versus a surgical robot (Istio — more capable, dramatically more complex to operate). If your surgery needs the robot, use Istio. If the scalpel does the job, the simpler tool is the better choice.
words.techContext: We chose Linkerd over Istio because our 2,000-pod cluster's memory budget was tight — Linkerd's micro-proxies added 10 MB each versus Envoy's 50-100 MB, saving 80+ GB of RAM across the fleet.
words.exampleSentence: After injecting Linkerd, we had automatic mTLS between all services and golden-signal dashboards for every route in Grafana — our security and observability requirements were met with a one-line annotation per namespace.

codeExample.code:
# Enable Linkerd injection for a namespace
kubectl annotate namespace payments \
  linkerd.io/inject=enabled

# Verify mesh injection and check mTLS status
linkerd check --proxy --namespace payments
linkerd viz stat deploy --namespace payments
# NAME          MESHED   SUCCESS      RPS   LATENCY_P99   ...
# checkout        1/1    99.82%   43.4rps        12ms
# payments-api    1/1    99.95%   39.1rps         8ms

words.etymology: Linkerd: a portmanteau of linker and daemon — the tool that links services together as a background process. Created by Buoyant Inc. (William Morgan and Oliver Gould) in 2016, the first tool to be called a 'service mesh'.

words.shortDefinition: Adjusts node count in a node group when pods are unschedulable (scale up) or nodes are underutilised (scale down).
words.simpleDefinition: Cluster Autoscaler (CA) is a Kubernetes component that watches for pods that cannot be scheduled due to insufficient node resources (scale up) and for nodes that have been underutilised for a configurable period (scale down). It adjusts the size of a cloud provider's node group (AWS ASG, GCP MIG, Azure VMSS) and works with the cloud provider API to provision or terminate nodes.
words.longDefinition: Cluster Autoscaler runs as a Deployment in the cluster and interfaces with both the Kubernetes API and the cloud provider's scaling API. Scale-up trigger: when the scheduler marks a pod as Unschedulable due to insufficient CPU, memory, or a required node label, CA identifies which node groups could accommodate the pod, simulates scheduling to verify, and increases the node group's desired count. A new node registers with the cluster in 1-5 minutes (depending on cloud provider and AMI). Scale-down trigger: CA periodically identifies nodes where all pods could be rescheduled onto other nodes while respecting PodDisruptionBudgets, taints, and affinity rules. A node that passes this check for the configurable `scale-down-unneeded-time` (default: 10 minutes) is drained and the cloud instance terminated. CA works with cloud-provider-specific node group configurations: AWS Auto Scaling Groups, GCP Managed Instance Groups, Azure VMSS. Its limitation versus Karpenter: CA scales within pre-defined node groups with fixed instance types — you must define separate groups for each instance family you want. This leads to over-provisioning (use a large instance family to handle any burst) or group sprawl (maintain many groups for different workload types). Karpenter addresses this by selecting instance type at scheduling time. CA remains the more mature solution for environments where node groups need to match specific compliance requirements or instance reservations.
words.connector: Cluster Autoscaler is like a property manager for a parking lot — when cars (pods) can't find spaces, she calls the lot owner to open another section (scale up node group); when a section has been mostly empty for 10 minutes, she cones it off and returns it to the owner (scale down).
words.techContext: Cluster Autoscaler's scale-down logic drained and terminated 12 underutilised nodes overnight, saving us 18% on our monthly EC2 bill without a single pod losing availability — the PodDisruptionBudget checks ensured minimum replicas were respected.
words.exampleSentence: After a traffic spike spun up 20 extra nodes, Cluster Autoscaler drained and terminated them over the following hour once load dropped — our compute cost tracked traffic precisely rather than staying provisioned for peak.

codeExample.code:
# Cluster Autoscaler Deployment (AWS EKS)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: cluster-autoscaler
  namespace: kube-system
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: cluster-autoscaler
          image: registry.k8s.io/autoscaling/cluster-autoscaler:v1.30.0
          command:
            - ./cluster-autoscaler
            - --cloud-provider=aws
            - --node-group-auto-discovery=asg:tag=k8s.io/cluster-autoscaler/enabled,k8s.io/cluster-autoscaler/my-cluster
            - --balance-similar-node-groups
            - --skip-nodes-with-system-pods=false
            - --scale-down-unneeded-time=10m

words.etymology: Cluster Autoscaler: descriptive name for the component that automatically scales the cluster's node count. Originated as a Kubernetes community project in 2016; maintained by SIG Autoscaling.

words.shortDefinition: Kubernetes device plugin model that exposes GPU counts as schedulable resources; DRA in 1.26+ improves fractional sharing.
words.simpleDefinition: GPU scheduling on Kubernetes uses the NVIDIA Device Plugin DaemonSet to advertise GPU devices as schedulable resources (`nvidia.com/gpu`). Pods request GPUs in their resource limits; the scheduler finds a node with available GPUs and the NVIDIA Container Runtime injects CUDA driver access. MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) hardware-partitions a single A100 into up to 7 isolated slices. DRA in 1.32+ extends this to richer allocation semantics including topology and sharing constraints.
words.longDefinition: ML workloads on Kubernetes require a pipeline of GPU-specific infrastructure. The NVIDIA Device Plugin (a DaemonSet) uses the Kubernetes Device Plugin API to discover GPUs via the NVML library, advertise them as `nvidia.com/gpu: N` resources, and assign specific devices to scheduled pods via device binding. The NVIDIA Container Runtime (a containerd/CRI-O shim that wraps runc) injects NVIDIA driver mounts and device nodes into the container before start — without it, CUDA initialization fails even if a GPU device is assigned. MIG (Multi-Instance GPU, introduced with Ampere A100) allows hardware partitioning of a single GPU into up to 7 isolated MIG instances, each with its own memory slice and compute slice. MIG instances appear as separate resources to Kubernetes (e.g., `nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb: 1`). This enables multiple inference workloads to share one $30,000 GPU with true hardware isolation. For pre-Ampere GPUs, time-slicing (advertising one GPU as N virtual GPUs sharing time) and NVIDIA MPS (Multi-Process Service, reducing context-switch overhead) provide sharing without hardware isolation. GPU fragmentation — a cluster with 8 GPUs but a pending pod requesting 8 on the same node, when GPUs are spread across 8 nodes — is a real operational problem. Volcano's gang scheduling and the NVIDIA GPU Operator's bin-packing scheduler plugin address fragmentation. The DRA API (GA in 1.32) replaces integer device counts with structured ResourceClaims, enabling topology-aware allocation such as 'two GPUs on the same NVLink fabric'.
words.connector: GPU scheduling is like managing premium hotel suites: the device plugin is the concierge who tracks available suites; MIG is like splitting a penthouse into separate rooms each sold independently; DRA is a reservation system that books specific rooms based on guest requirements (window facing east, adjacent to room 101).
words.techContext: After enabling MIG on our A100 nodes with the NVIDIA GPU Operator, we went from 4 concurrent training jobs (each consuming a whole GPU) to 28 concurrent inference jobs (each using a 1g.10gb MIG slice) — a 7x improvement in GPU utilisation.
words.exampleSentence: GPU scheduling with MIG let us run 7 independent ML inference workloads on a single A100, each with hardware-isolated memory, instead of serialising them or buying 7 separate GPU instances.

codeExample.code:
# Pod requesting a MIG GPU slice (1g.10gb = 1/7 of an A100)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: inference-server
spec:
  containers:
    - name: server
      image: nvcr.io/nvidia/tritonserver:24.01-py3
      resources:
        limits:
          nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb: 1  # one MIG slice
      env:
        - name: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES
          valueFrom:
            fieldRef:
              fieldPath: metadata.annotations['nvidia.com/gpu-assigned']

words.etymology: GPU (Graphics Processing Unit): coined by NVIDIA's marketing team for the GeForce 256 launch in 1999 to distinguish the highly parallel compute chip from the CPU. GPU scheduling as a Kubernetes concept emerged with the device plugin API in Kubernetes 1.8 (2017).

words.shortDefinition: Immutable, minimal Linux OS designed exclusively for Kubernetes nodes; managed entirely via API, no SSH shell.
words.simpleDefinition: Talos Linux is an immutable Linux distribution whose only purpose is running Kubernetes nodes. The OS has no SSH daemon, no shell, no package manager, and no writable filesystem — every configuration change is made via an authenticated gRPC API (talosctl). This dramatically reduces the attack surface: there is no SSH vulnerability to exploit, no package to be compromised, and no interactive session for an attacker to persist in.
words.longDefinition: Traditional Kubernetes nodes run a general-purpose Linux distribution (Ubuntu, RHEL, Amazon Linux) with all the associated attack surface: SSH daemons, cron jobs, package managers, and interactive login shells. Talos Linux (Sidero Labs, 2018) removes all of this. The OS image is a read-only squashfs partition containing only the Linux kernel, the container runtime (containerd), the kubelet, and the Talos API server (apid). All disk partitions except /var (ephemeral data) and /etc/kubernetes (config) are immutable. Node configuration (kubelet flags, network settings, cluster membership) is declared in a YAML machine config and applied via `talosctl apply-config` — delivered over the Talos API with mutual TLS. There is no persistent SSH daemon; emergency access is via the serial console only. Upgrades are atomic: Talos downloads a new OS image, writes it to the spare A/B partition, and reboots into it — if the new partition fails to boot, it falls back automatically. Integration with Cluster API (CAPI) and Omni (Sidero's hosted management plane) provides fleet management for Talos clusters. The immutable, API-driven model maps cleanly to GitOps workflows: the desired OS state is a version-controlled machine config file. Talos Linux is increasingly popular for air-gapped, security-sensitive, and edge environments where the attack surface of a general-purpose OS is unacceptable. It is not appropriate for nodes where engineers need interactive debugging sessions.
words.connector: Talos Linux is like a car's ECU (Engine Control Unit) — you cannot pop the hood and reprogram it with a USB drive; all changes go through the official diagnostic interface with authenticated commands, and the firmware is read-only by design.
words.techContext: After migrating to Talos Linux for our edge Kubernetes nodes, our quarterly security audit removed the entire SSH daemon vulnerability category from scope — there is no SSH to configure, patch, or exploit.
words.exampleSentence: A Talos Linux node has no shell and no SSH, so when the security team ran their standard port scan looking for management interfaces, they found nothing — every config change goes through the authenticated Talos gRPC API.

codeExample.code:
# Generate Talos machine config for a control-plane node
talosctl gen config my-cluster https://10.0.0.1:6443 \
  --config-patch-control-plane @patches/controlplane.yaml

# Apply config to a node (mutual TLS, no SSH)
talosctl apply-config \
  --nodes 10.0.0.10 \
  --file controlplane.yaml

# Upgrade node OS atomically (A/B partition flip)
talosctl upgrade \
  --nodes 10.0.0.10 \
  --image ghcr.io/siderolabs/installer:v1.8.0

words.etymology: Talos: named after Talos, the giant bronze automaton of Greek mythology who guarded the island of Crete — an autonomous, unstoppable sentinel with no human-accessible interface. Created by Andrew Rynhard at Autonomy Squared (later Sidero Labs) in 2018.

words.shortDefinition: OCI-compatible runtime that wraps each container in a lightweight VM for hypervisor-level isolation without changing workload images.
words.simpleDefinition: Kata Containers is an OCI-compatible container runtime that runs each pod inside a lightweight virtual machine (using QEMU, Firecracker, or cloud-hypervisor as the VMM). From Kubernetes' perspective, a Kata pod looks like any other container. From a security perspective, the container process runs inside a dedicated VM kernel — a container escape only reaches the lightweight VM, not the host.
words.longDefinition: Standard containers share the host kernel — a kernel exploit inside a container is a host compromise. Kata Containers (CNCF Incubating, formed by merging Intel Clear Containers and Hyper.sh runV in 2017) solves this by using a hypervisor to give each pod its own kernel. The architecture: the Kata runtime (kata-runtime) implements the OCI runtime spec. When containerd creates a Kata pod, kata-runtime launches a VMM (QEMU, Firecracker, or cloud-hypervisor) that boots a stripped-down Linux kernel in a VM in ~100-200 ms. The container's rootfs is shared into the VM via virtio-fs or virtio-9p. A kata-agent process inside the VM's kernel manages container lifecycle on behalf of containerd outside the VM, communicating over vsock. To Kubernetes, this looks like a normal pod — the same YAML, the same kubectl commands, the same metrics. The isolation is transparent to the workload. Performance overhead: ~100-200 ms additional cold start, ~5-15% CPU overhead for I/O-heavy workloads due to virtio drivers, ~50-200 MB additional memory per pod for the VM kernel. Firecracker (AWS) reduces this to ~125 ms startup and ~5 MB overhead per microVM but lacks some Linux features. Kata is the runtime substrate for confidential containers — combining a Kata VM with AMD SEV-SNP or Intel TDX gives both VM isolation and memory encryption. RuntimeClass enables mixed workloads: most pods use runc; pods that handle untrusted user data or require strong isolation use kata-runtime, specified in `runtimeClassName: kata`.
words.connector: Standard containers are like office cubicles — same building, shared walls, a determined person could climb over. Kata Containers are like individual offices with locked doors and separate ventilation — you still share the same building address (Kubernetes API), but a break-in to one office cannot directly access another.
words.techContext: We use Kata Containers for our user-code execution service — customer-submitted scripts run in Kata pods, so a container escape reaches only the lightweight VM kernel, not our multi-tenant node's filesystem and credentials.
words.exampleSentence: Switching our CI runner pods to Kata Containers eliminated the security concern about user-supplied Dockerfiles — a malicious build step that escapes the container is contained within a Kata microVM, not the build node.

codeExample.code:
# RuntimeClass for Kata (configured during node setup)
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: kata
handler: kata  # containerd runtime handler name
overhead:
  podFixed:
    memory: 160Mi   # VM kernel overhead per pod

words.etymology: Kata: from the Japanese martial arts term for a structured practice form — implying a disciplined, structured approach to container isolation. The project merged Intel's Clear Containers project and Hyper.sh's runV at KubeCon 2017 under the OpenStack Foundation (now Open Infrastructure Foundation).

words.shortDefinition: Cloud-provider-operated control planes that handle upgrades, etcd, and master HA so operators focus on node pools and workloads.
words.simpleDefinition: Managed Kubernetes services (AWS EKS, Google GKE, Azure AKS) operate the Kubernetes control plane — API server, etcd, controller manager, scheduler — as a fully managed cloud service. The operator never SSHes into a control-plane node, manages etcd backups, or provisions master HA. The operator manages node pools (instance types, sizes, versions) and workloads. EKS, GKE, and AKS are the three dominant platforms and account for the majority of production Kubernetes deployments globally.
words.longDefinition: Self-managed Kubernetes (kubeadm, k3s, Cluster API) requires the operator to manage etcd backups, control-plane HA (typically 3 master nodes), certificate rotation, API server load balancers, and version upgrades — a significant operational burden. Managed services eliminate this by running the control plane on cloud-provider infrastructure and billing per cluster-hour. Key differences across the three major providers: AWS EKS operates a multi-tenant control plane per region; etcd and API servers run in AWS-managed accounts. Node pools are EC2 instances (EKS Managed Node Groups, Karpenter, or Fargate for serverless). EKS typically lags the upstream K8s release by 1-3 months. EKS's strength is deep AWS service integration (IAM Roles for Service Accounts, ALB Ingress Controller, EBS/EFS CSI, Karpenter). Google GKE pioneered managed Kubernetes (GKE Alpha in 2014, GA in 2015) and remains the most feature-rich managed platform. Autopilot mode manages node pools automatically. GKE Dataplane V2 (Cilium eBPF) is the default since 2021. GKE has the fastest K8s version release cadence. Azure AKS provides the deepest integration with Azure Active Directory (OIDC federation for workload identity), Azure Policy (OPA Gatekeeper integration), and Azure Monitor. AKS has a free control-plane tier (only node VM costs). In 2026, the platform choice for most teams is cloud-native managed K8s unless there is a specific reason (air-gap, non-cloud bare-metal, multi-cloud portability) to operate the control plane directly.
words.connector: Managed Kubernetes is like leasing office space versus owning a building. Self-managed Kubernetes means maintaining the HVAC, electricity, security, and elevators yourself. EKS/GKE/AKS are landlords who handle building infrastructure — you focus on what happens in your rented offices (node pools and workloads).
words.techContext: Moving to GKE Autopilot eliminated our biggest operational toil: we no longer specify node pool instance types or manage cluster capacity — GKE provisions and scales nodes automatically per workload request, and we pay only for what pods actually consume.
words.exampleSentence: EKS handled the Kubernetes 1.30 upgrade by live-upgrading the managed control plane with zero downtime — our only task was to update node groups on our own schedule within the 14-month support window.

codeExample.code:
# Create an EKS cluster with managed node group (eksctl)
eksctl create cluster \
  --name production \
  --region us-east-1 \
  --version 1.30 \
  --nodegroup-name general \
  --node-type m7g.xlarge \
  --nodes 3 \
  --nodes-min 1 \
  --nodes-max 20 \
  --managed

# Update control plane version (zero-downtime)
eksctl upgrade cluster --name production --version 1.31 --approve

words.etymology: EKS: Elastic Kubernetes Service. GKE: Google Kubernetes Engine. AKS: Azure Kubernetes Service. All follow the cloud provider's naming conventions (Elastic/Google/Azure + Kubernetes + Service/Engine). GKE was the first managed Kubernetes service, launched in 2014 before Kubernetes 1.0.
